title: Here’s Why It’s So Hard to Boost a Satellite - Nautilus
gist: NASA's Swift Observatory reentered over Indonesia on Nov. 4, 2026 after orbital decay ended its mission, months after the commercial LINK robotic rescue spacecraft meant to boost it reentered first — illustrating how hard satellite rescue and servicing remain.

themes.theme: Swift loss and failed commercial rescue

insights.claim: NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory took its last observation on Oct. 20, 2026 at about 171 miles altitude, and NASA ended the mission three days later because atmospheric drag kept its telescopes from holding steady.
insights.so_what: Orbital decay is a hard limit on low-orbit asset lifetimes.

insights.speaker: Wanjiku Chebet Kanjumba

insights.claim: Swift reentered the atmosphere on Nov. 4, 2026 above Indonesia's North Sumatra region and largely burned up, ending two decades of observing cosmic explosions.
insights.locator: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory took
insights.speaker: Wanjiku Chebet Kanjumba

insights.claim: LINK, a commercial robotic spacecraft sent in summer 2026 to raise Swift to a safer orbit, failed and itself reentered Earth's atmosphere in September, before Swift.
insights.so_what: A visible setback for the commercial in-orbit servicing/life-extension sector.
insights.quote: The machine designed to save a falling satellite burned up first.

insights.speaker: Wanjiku Chebet Kanjumba

insights.claim: An aerospace engineering researcher who studies spacecraft approach and capture argues rescuing satellites is hard, especially capturing objects that tumble uncontrollably.
insights.so_what: Temper expectations for near-term in-orbit servicing business models.
insights.quote: I know that rescuing satellites is hard
